steps.tx: To prevent catastrophic occlusive thrombosis following vascular sealing, the body utilizes an endogenous enzymatic clot-dissolving mechanism designated **fibrinolysis**. The principal fibrinolytic enzyme is the serine protease plasmin, which cleaves insoluble fibrin polymers into soluble degradation fragments, restoring microvascular vessel patency as tissue repair proceeds.
steps.say: Fibrinolysis dissolves clots to restore vessel patency. Plasmin cleaves insoluble fibrin into soluble degradation fragments during tissue repair.

nodes.label: Endothelial Cells Synthesize and Secrete Tissue Plasminogen Activator (tPA)
tPA Binds Fibrin Clot and Cleaves Trapped Plasminogen into Active Plasmin
Plasmin Hydrolyses Insoluble Fibrin Meshwork into Soluble Degradation Products
Covalently Cross-Linked Fibrin Breakdown Generates Measurable D-Dimers

steps.tx: Inactive circulating plasminogen binds avidly to lysine residues within the cross-linked fibrin clot. Endothelial cells synthesize **tissue plasminogen activator** (tPA), which binds fibrin-associated plasminogen with high catalytic efficiency, cleaving the arginine-valine bond to generate active plasmin locally within the thrombus while minimizing systemic free plasmin circulation.
steps.say: Endothelial tissue plasminogen activator cleaves clot-bound plasminogen into active plasmin, concentrating fibrinolysis inside the clot to prevent systemic bleeding.

steps.tx: When plasmin digests cross-linked fibrin stabilized by Factor XIIIa, it generates specific breakdown fragments containing intact covalent gamma-chain cross-links, designated **D-dimer**. Elevation of plasma D-dimer indicates active in vivo thrombin generation and subsequent fibrinolysis, serving as a high-sensitivity screening biomarker to rule out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
steps.say: Plasmin digestion of cross-linked fibrin generates D-dimers. Elevated D-dimer confirms active clotting and breakdown, used to exclude pulmonary embolism.

steps.tx: Uncontrolled systemic clotting is constrained by endogenous anticoagulant cascades. The most potent circulating inhibitor of thrombin and Factor Xa is **antithrombin** (antithrombin III). Synthesized by hepatocytes, antithrombin is an alpha-2 globulin that suicide-inhibits serine proteases. Endothelial heparan sulfate proteoglycans accelerate antithrombin inhibitory kinetics one thousand-fold, a mechanism mirrored by clinical heparin therapy.
steps.say: Antithrombin suicide-inhibits thrombin and Factor Xa. Endothelial heparan sulfate accelerates this reaction a thousand-fold, a mechanism mimicked by heparin.

rows: Suicide substrate forming 1:1 complex; heparin accelerated

steps.tx: A second critical regulatory brake is the **protein C** pathway. Thrombin binds to the endothelial transmembrane receptor thrombomodulin, undergoing a conformational change that abolishes its procoagulant actions. The thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates circulating vitamin K-dependent Protein C, which pairs with its cofactor Protein S on endothelial surfaces to proteolytically inactivate Factors Va and VIIIa.
steps.say: Thrombin binds thrombomodulin to activate Protein C, which pairs with Protein S to proteolytically destroy cofactors Va and VIIIa, halting coagulation.

steps.tx: Post-translational gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues on Factors II, VII, IX, and X, alongside regulatory Proteins C and S, requires **vitamin K** as an essential cofactor. Reduced vitamin K hydroquinone powers gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, adding a carboxyl group to create dicarboxylic Gla domains that bind calcium to anchor onto platelet membranes. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking this activation.
steps.say: Vitamin K gamma-carboxylates glutamic acid residues on Factors II, VII, IX, and X, allowing calcium binding. Warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling.

left.title: Carboxylated Factors (Functional)
points: Contain paired negative carboxyl charges on Gla residues
Anchor firmly onto platelet negatively charged phospholipids
Assemble tenase and prothrombinase catalytic complexes

right.title: Des-Carboxy Factors (Warfarin Induced)
points: Remain floating in plasma; cannot bind platelet membrane
Functionally inactive, producing systemic therapeutic anticoagulation

steps.tx: Congenital deficiency of intrinsic pathway factors causes classic haemophilia. **Haemophilia A** is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by deficiency of Factor VIII, while Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is caused by Factor IX deficiency. Because the intrinsic tenase complex is crippled, patients suffer deep tissue bleeds, painful recurrent hemarthroses leading to joint destruction, and marked isolated aPTT prolongation.
steps.say: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked deficiencies of Factors VIII and IX respectively, causing hemarthroses and deep tissue haematomas with isolated aPTT prolongation.

vis.caption: Factor VIII and Factor IX deficiencies and joint bleeding in haemophilia. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Treatment of haemophilia requires recombinant factor replacement to restore clotting competence. Recombinant Factor VIII concentrates are infused on demand or prophylactically. In mild Haemophilia A, **desmopressin** (DDAVP) stimulates endothelial V2 receptors, releasing endogenous stores of Factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from Weibel-Palade bodies into plasma to arrest bleeding.
steps.say: Haemophilia is managed with recombinant factor concentrates. Mild Haemophilia A responds to desmopressin, which mobilises stored Factor VIII and vWF from endothelia.
